861.quote_or_event: “O king, bring into subjection all princes who do not acknowledge you; thus you will be a true Kshattriya.” … “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
861.explanation: Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges the renouncing King Nami to subdue the weaker princes around him as a true warrior should. Nami refuses and says the only conquest worth seeking is conquest of oneself.
861.tie_back: The Kural advises a ruler to pick fights only with weaker foes, and the Jain text puts that same advice in Indra's mouth and has the saint reject it, so the passage answers the Kural's strategy rather than echoing it.
861.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.32 and 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
861._accuracy_note: Both verses checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (9.33 is only a speaker tag and is omitted). The passage deals with the Kural's subject but takes the opposite position, because ahimsa rules out seeking enmity even with the weak, so it is scored as a next-best match.

862.quote_or_event: “Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.”
862.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana teaches that no kinsman or ally can shield a soul from the fruit of its own karma, so the seeker must rely on his own conduct.
862.tie_back: The Kural says a man without loving kin, strong allies or strength of his own cannot break an enemy. The Jain verse agrees that relying on others fails, but it moves the struggle inward, where only one's own strength counts.
862.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 6.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
862._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Only a partial and partly opposed parallel: the Kural praises kin and allies as political assets, while the Jain verse says they are of no help against karma.

863.quote_or_event: “Weak men who are unable (to bear) these insults in villages or towns, become disheartened like cowards in the battle.”
863.explanation: In its chapter on the hardships of monastic life, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga compares the faint-hearted novice, who breaks under insult and hardship, to a coward who loses heart once the battle begins.
863.tie_back: The Kural calls the fearful man easy prey for his enemies, and the Jain verse likewise shows timidity defeating a man before any real foe has to strike.
863.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.3.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
863._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi's translation on wisdomlib.org. It matches only the first of the Kural's four faults (fear) and is about inner hardships, not human enemies; ignorance, lack of accord and stinginess are not covered.

864.quote_or_event: “He should not give way to his anger, and bear with indifference pleasant and unpleasant occurrences. Subdue your Self, for the Self is difficult to subdue; if your Self is subdued, you will be happy in this world and in the next. Better it is that I should subdue my Self by self-control and penance, than be subdued by others with fetters and corporal punishment.”
864.explanation: Mahāvīra's discipline joins the curbing of anger with mastery of the self, and warns that whoever does not subdue himself will be subdued by others.
864.tie_back: The Kural says a man of lasting anger and no inner restraint (nirai) can be beaten by anyone, and these verses give the same pairing, adding that the self-mastered person cannot be overpowered from outside.
864.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.14–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
864._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; the quotation begins partway through 1.14. A strong thematic fit (anger plus self-restraint, and being subdued by others), though the setting is monastic discipline rather than enmity.

865.quote_or_event: “Benighted men of wrong faith, (though) they be renowned as heroes, exert themselves in a bad way, which will have, in all respects, evil consequences for them.”
865.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga contrasts the effort of those who lack right faith and follow a wrong path, which brings them only ruin, with the effort of the wise who follow the right path.
865.tie_back: The Kural says a man who does not look to the right path or do what is fitting delights his enemies, and the Jain verse likewise says that effort cut off from the right path brings about its own downfall.
865.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
865._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. It matches the Kural's 'not looking to the right path' but has nothing on disgrace or on enemies taking advantage, so it is a partial match.

866.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space. … He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
866.explanation: King Nami describes desire as boundless as space and says that the person ruled by anger, pride, delusion and greed brings about his own fall.
866.tie_back: The Kural welcomes as an enemy the man blinded by anger and swollen with boundless desire because he will destroy himself, and Nami describes exactly that self-ruin through anger and limitless craving.
866.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.48 and 9.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
866._accuracy_note: Both verses checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (sacred-texts writes Kailâsa). A close match for the Kural's anger, boundless desire and self-destruction; the Kural's point that such a man makes a welcome enemy has no Jain counterpart.

867.quote_or_event: “Now this driver (viz. Garga), who had to deal with bad bullocks, thought: 'What have I to do with bad pupils? I am disheartened. As are bad pupils, so are bad bullocks; I shall leave these lazy donkeys, and shall practise severe austerities.'”
867.explanation: The elder Garga, worn out by disciples who stayed close to him yet behaved unworthily, breaks with them completely and goes on alone, accepting the loss of his following.
867.tie_back: The Kural says one should break even at a cost with someone who stays close yet acts unworthily, and Garga does this by giving up his whole following rather than keep company with bad pupils.
867.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 27.15–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
867._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. Garga separates from his pupils without turning them into enemies, and the Kural's 'even at a price' is only implied by his loss of a following, so this is a partial match.

868.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out.”
868.explanation: The opening lecture of the Uttarādhyayana says that a monk of bad character finds no welcome anywhere and is driven out of every community.
868.tie_back: The Kural says a man with no virtues and many faults ends up without allies, and the Jain simile shows the same result: faults leave a man unwanted and alone.
868.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
868._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It matches the step from faults to friendlessness but does not go on, as the Kural does, to say that this isolation strengthens one's enemies.

869.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe, as did Śiśupāla (before he beheld) the valorously-fighting, great warrior. They go forward to the head of the battle; but when the fight has begun the mother will not recognise her son, and he will be mangled by his foe.”
869.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga uses the image of a boastful but untried fighter who collapses once he faces a real opponent, as a warning to novice monks who overrate their own strength.
869.tie_back: The Kural says those who fight are glad to meet foes who are foolish and fearful, and the Jain image of the vain warrior who is crushed in his first real encounter shows exactly that kind of foe.
869.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.3.1.1–2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
869._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. The battle image fits the foolish, fearful enemy well, but the text uses it only as a parable for monastic hardship and does not endorse the victor's joy that the Kural describes.

870.quote_or_event: “Penance is of no good if performed by noble men who have turned monks (for the sake of fame); but that penance of which nobody else knows anything (is meritorious). Do not spread your own fame!”
870.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga denies that seeking glory has any spiritual worth and says that hidden, unadvertised effort is the only kind that counts.
870.tie_back: The Kural says glory never comes to the man who will not take the easy gain of opposing an unlearned foe, while the Jain verse tells the seeker not to pursue glory at all, an honest contrast rather than a parallel.
870.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.8.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
870._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. No Jain text recommends gaining fame by attacking the unlearned, so this is a next-best, contrasting match on the theme of glory.
